content:
Hi, with Tuomo Kuusi we formalized some of our own work on quantitative homogenization and coarse-graining theory for elliptic PDEs. Our git repo is here: https://github.com/scottnarmstrong/CoarseGraining

I made a short blog post announcing it here: https://www.scottnarmstrong.com/2026/06/formalizing-stochastic-homogenization-in-lean/

The total amount of lean code is 449k lines, 1200 files, it compiles in 26 min on an 8-core ubuntu machine. There are zero sorries/axioms/etc.

We took one result one could consider "the main result" and set it up with comparator, also in the repo. It is a bit difficult to use comparator in this case since the definitions themselves are nontrivial to write from mathlib. But, we are sure that the formalization is correct.

The development was entirely written by GPT 5.5 with some small contribution from Opus 4.X.

Any criticisms and/or suggestions would be welcome if anyone wanted to take a look at what we did.

Given the ~600 lines of non-mathlib definitions in the Challenge.lean file, it is difficult to parse the exact statement which is proven here. Would it be possible to formulate some non-trivial corollaries of the main result which require fewer definitions? This could be nice to have as a sanity check, and to convince the reader that the result is not accidentally vacuous.

Nevertheless, I think it is very cool that results in this direction can be formalized with current technology.

Given the ~600 lines of non-mathlib definitions in the Challenge.lean file, it is difficult to parse the exact statement which is proven here

Yes, this is what Opus 4.8 predicted would be the first comment.

The answer is no, you cannot formulate a better non-trivial corollaries, in fact the comparator statement is the nontrivial corollary. The actual theorems are much stronger and more general.

PDE statements require definitions which are not in mathlib, like the definition of Sobolev space, and definition of weak solution... these very very basic things are unfortunately basically totally absent in mathlib, so the comparator file needs them to be built in the challenge file.

Maybe it is possible to do better, but this statement is really the best I could do. I tried.

Is it important to work with weak solutions here, or would an estimate for strong/smooth solutions have essentially the same content? (sorry I am not familiar with the paper). If yes, this could already lead to a simplified statement.

Hmm.. I guess you could work with strong/classical solutions, but this would be a weird statement because a general equation will not have such solutions unless you assume the coefficients are qualitatively smooth. It did not occur to me to do this, but I think it would be possible to write such a statement -- even though weird it might be easier to check. I suppose it would not be difficult for an LLM to do this. Let me try to do it and get back to you, thanks for the suggestion. (You will still have to get through all the definitions relating to the stationary random field and the probabilistic assumptions however!)
Ok, and I will also try to demonstrate that you can get a periodic homogenization result out as a corollary, which collapses all the randomness.

This is really cool.

Do you think it would be possible to draw a line (through the manuscript and/or the repository) that says "everything below this line is the obviously reusable stuff, that any researcher who went to the same conferences as me would agree we need" (and conversely everything above that line is somehow "paper specific")?

(I know that analysts like to say they have no theorems, only examples, but for the sake of the argument let's be ambitious about reusability here. :-)

What's the most condensed form you could convey that information to me? A list of section numbers in the manuscript? A list of Lean files in the repo?

I would love to have this information extracted out of your project.

I pushed an update to the repo which fixes the measurability API (which was not completely ok) and adds four comparator challenges for a total of five. The comparators are now:

1) the general statement from before
2) a special case of periodic coefficient fields (the probability measure is a Dirac)
3) a very special case of a particular periodic field (there is a simple formula)
4) the same particular periodic field but now the solutions are classical
5) a random checkerboard (the simplest possible random example, just to make sure that some random example is also possible)

All are proved by invoking the much more general theorems in the repo, and all comparator challenges are confirmed "Your solution is okay!"

Hopefully this shows that something non-vacuous is going on, and I really thank Joris van Winden for the suggestion because forcing me to do that improved the code.

If there are any other suggestions for making this transparent, I'd be happy to hear them.

Kim: I need to think about (and remember) exactly what background material I had to develop. My feeling is that you won't want to reuse directly anything here, but maybe pointing agents at the repo might help speed things up. I had to develop a bunch of function space things, but the particular results and definitions I needed are quite particular and suited for my particular needs. Maybe there is a nice proof of some Sobolev things on general convex domains, but I think this is also being developed elsewhere and is not very difficult. Most of the repo is formalizing the particular theory we have developed in our papers over the last ten years.
